strengths: The paper addresses a clear and well-motivated gap: existing LSNM-based causal discovery methods assume symmetric noise, and the authors convincingly demonstrate (Fig. 1, Fig. 2) that skewed noise breaks these methods, both intuition-wise via residual analysis and empirically.

SKEWD is a technically careful extension of the skew-normal LSNM framework: penalized B-spline likelihoods, a hybrid CMA-ES + ECM optimization that addresses known pathologies of skew-normal maximum likelihood (unbounded likelihood, stationary points), with an ablation (Tabs. 2-3) showing the ECM refinement is genuinely necessary (up to 34% improvement for the IT variant).

Evaluation is broad and transparent: novel synthetic benchmarks spanning multiple skewness levels and two noise families (skew-normal and GNO), plus 13 established benchmarks (AN/LS/SIM/Tübingen/Cha/Net/Multi) with 11 baselines, and exact per-dataset results in the appendix.
The method performs on par with SOTA on established benchmarks (Tab. 1, 8) while being the only method with perfect accuracy under high skewness, matching the central claim.
Code and data are released, and the limitations section is honest about scope (bivariate only, bounded skewness of the skew-normal family, Gaussian marginal assumption for likelihood scoring).
weaknesses: The novel benchmark construction raises concerns about difficulty and potential bias: SKEWD-LL achieves 100% accuracy on all six skew-noise datasets, and the strongly misspecified IGCI-G also achieves near-perfect accuracy (100/100/100/100/99.5/100), suggesting the sigmoidal, injective data-generating mechanisms may make the task nearly solvable by simple heuristics. This weakens the evidence that SKEWD's advantage stems specifically from modeling skewness.

A conceptual tension is not adequately addressed: the skew-normal distribution's skewness is bounded by ~0.995, yet SKEWD-LL achieves perfect accuracy on datasets with skewness 1.750 (GNO noise) that lie outside its model class. Some discussion of why the method generalizes beyond its assumptions would strengthen the contribution.

The likelihood-scoring variant relies on a Gaussian marginal assumption (with an asymptotic argument in Prop. 1 that is essentially trivial), and this shows in practice: on the real-world Tübingen benchmark SKEWD-LL scores 45.97% accuracy, below chance. The practical relevance of SKEWD-LL outside synthetic data is thus questionable, while SKEWD-IT is not the top performer on skewed data in absolute terms.

No runtime or computational cost comparison is provided, despite a heavy pipeline (Bayesian optimization over penalty parameters with 8-fold cross-validation, multiple CMA-ES runs, plus ECM refinement per direction per pair). This is a significant practical concern for adopting the method.

Theoretical novelty is limited: identifiability is inherited from existing results (restated in Appendix A), and the ECM algorithm is a modification of Ferreira et al. (2023). The contribution is primarily a careful adaptation plus empirical study.

Minor presentation issues: inconsistent naming (SkewD vs. SKEWD), a typo in the ablation text ('CMA-ES-LL and CMA-ES-LL'), Fig. 2 y-axis labels appear duplicated, and no statistical significance analysis accompanies the mean±std comparisons in Tab. 1 where the top methods differ by ~2.7%.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated gap: existing LSNM-based causal discovery methods (LOCI, QCCD, likelihood scorers) assume symmetric noise, and the paper convincingly demonstrates that skewed noise degrades their reliability (Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Tab. 4).

The technical machinery is carefully developed: the penalized spline skew-normal LSNM, the CMA-ES initialization refined by an ECM algorithm (adapted from Ferreira et al. 2023), and the Bayesian-optimization step for penalty parameters are all described in enough detail to implement, with hyperparameters fully specified in Appendix B.

The empirical evaluation is broad: novel skew-noise datasets at three skewness levels plus 13 established benchmarks (AN/LS/SIM/Tübingen/Cha/Net/Multi), with both accuracy and AUDRC, an ablation of the ECM refinement (Tab. 2/3), and full per-dataset tables in the appendix.

The ablation (Tab. 2/3) genuinely demonstrates the necessity of the ECM refinement step (up to 28–34% improvement for the independence-test variant), rather than leaving the two-stage optimizer as an unmotivated design choice.
The paper is honest about limitations (bivariate only, heavy tails not handled, Gaussian marginal assumption for likelihood scoring) and provides code for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central benchmark is self-serving: the novel ANs/LSs datasets are generated exactly within the skew-normal LSNM class that SKEWD assumes, so the perfect 100% accuracy of SKEWD-LL (Tab. 4) largely confirms that fitting the true model class works, rather than demonstrating robustness to realistic misspecification. Notably, SKEWD-LL also scores 100% on the GNO-generated subsets with skewness γ1 ≈ 1.750 that provably exceeds the skew-normal's maximum skewness (≈0.995), which raises the question of whether the gains stem from skewness modeling at all or from a directional bias of likelihood scoring under heteroscedasticity — the authors themselves concede that the strongly misspecified IGCI-G also achieves ~100% on these datasets and 'seems to be biased toward the correct direction.'

On the established (neutral) benchmarks, SKEWD does not beat the state of the art: ROCHE is best on both accuracy and AUDRC in Tab. 1 and Tab. 8, and SKEWD-LL trails LOCI-LL on several datasets (e.g., MNU: 87 vs 100). The contribution therefore reduces to a specialized robustness improvement, and the advantage over ROCHE/t-noise modeling for skewed-but-not-heavy-tailed settings is not isolated experimentally.

The likelihood-scoring variant rests on a fragile argument: the marginal log-likelihoods are claimed negligible via Proposition 1, but this treats standardized skewed variables as approximately standard normal. The sum-of-squares identity (n−1) does hold for any standardized data, but the resulting normal marginal model is misspecified for the skewed effect variable, and the paper does not analyze how this misspecification interacts with the direction decision.

The computational pipeline is heavy — Bayesian optimization over penalty parameters with 8-fold cross-validation, multiple CMA-ES restarts, then ECM refinement, per direction per pair — yet no runtime or scalability comparison against baselines is reported. This matters for a method whose main selling point is reliability rather than capability.

No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals for the accuracy comparisons; with 100 pairs per synthetic dataset, differences such as SKEWD-IT (98.5%) vs ROCHE (99.5%) are within noise, making several comparative claims in Sec. 6 hard to evaluate.

Novelty is incremental: the model and ECM machinery are direct adaptations of Ferreira and Paula (2017) and Ferreira et al. (2023) to the LSNM setting, and the inference procedures (HSIC-based independence testing, likelihood comparison) are standard. The skew-normal family is also a fairly restrictive way to capture asymmetry (bounded skewness < 0.9953), which sits uneasily with the paper's framing of 'robustness under high skewness.'

The generalization claim in the conclusion ('most reliable approach for LSNMs under high skewness') is supported only by the synthetic data discussed above; no real-world dataset with genuinely skewed noise is analyzed to substantiate the motivating claim that skewness 'is likely in real-world domains' beyond citations.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing LSNM-based causal discovery methods (LOCI, QCCD, etc.) assume symmetric noise, and the paper convincingly demonstrates both theoretically motivated and empirically that skewness induces misspecification that breaks cause-effect inference (Fig. 1, Fig. 3).

The proposed method is technically well-grounded: the skew-normal LSNM extends the identifiable LSNM class while containing the Gaussian model as a special case, and the estimation pipeline (Bayesian optimization of penalty parameters -> CMA-ES heuristic -> ECM refinement) is carefully engineered and appropriately justified (ECM maintains the penalized likelihood ascent property, and the ablation in Tables 2-3 demonstrates that the ECM refinement step is genuinely necessary, particularly for independence testing).

Evaluation is unusually thorough: novel synthetic benchmarks spanning multiple skewness levels (including noise distributions beyond the skew-normal family via GNO), 13 established benchmarks, both accuracy and AUDRC metrics, multiple baselines from different model classes, and full tabulated results in the appendix.

The manuscript is clearly written, well-organized, and the limitations (bivariate-only, skew-normal skewness bound |gamma1| < 0.995, Gaussian marginal assumption for likelihood scoring) are honestly acknowledged. Code is stated to be publicly released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core contribution is somewhat incremental: the skew-normal machinery (EM/ECM estimation for skew-normal partially linear models) largely adapts Ferreira et al. (2023)/Ferreira and Paula (2017) to the LSNM setting with spline-based scale modeling, and the identifiability discussion (Appendix A, Theorem 1) restates Immer et al. (2023) rather than providing new theory specific to the skew-normal case.

There is a conceptual tension in the evaluation: the skew-normal distribution caps skewness at |gamma1| ~ 0.995, yet the headline results include datasets with gamma1 = 1.750 where the model is misspecified — and SKEWD-LL nonetheless reports perfect (100%) accuracy on all six synthetic datasets. This perfect score, together with IGCI-G (a strongly misspecified method) also achieving near-perfect accuracy on the same datasets, suggests the proposed sigmoidal-injective-function benchmark may be insufficiently discriminative, and the paper does not analyze why SKEWD succeeds on noise it cannot represent.

The central robustness claim rests primarily on the authors' own newly generated benchmark; on the 13 established benchmarks (Table 1 and Table 8), ROCHE outperforms both SKEWD variants on average, so SKEWD is a strong competitor but not clearly SOTA outside the skewed-noise setting.

Likelihood scoring assumes Gaussian marginals for the cause, and the standardization argument (Proposition 1) only holds asymptotically and only when the cause truly is normal; the sensitivity of SKEWD-LL to violation of this assumption is not empirically characterized. The heavy computational pipeline (Bayesian optimization + multi-start CMA-ES + ECM per direction per pair) also raises runtime concerns, but no runtime comparison against baselines is provided.

Noise-free error bars/seed-level variance are missing: standard deviations in Table 1 are across datasets, and with ~100 pairs per synthetic dataset, differences of a few percent (e.g., SKEWD-IT 85.02 vs. LOCI-IT 84.09 on established benchmarks) are not assessed for statistical significance.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper convincingly demonstrates (Figures 1, 3) that likelihood/independence-based LSNM methods fail under skewed noise, an assumption commonly made in prior work but frequently violated in practice.

Technically sound estimation methodology: the skew-normal LSNM with penalized likelihood and an ECM algorithm (adapted from Ferreira et al. 2023 to GAMs and location-scale models), including the latent-variable representation, E-step and CM-step derivations, is carefully derived, and an ablation (Tables 3-4) substantiates the claimed necessity of the ECM refinement over the CMA-ES heuristic.

Comprehensive and transparent empirical evaluation: the paper introduces novel skew-noise benchmarks spanning multiple skewness levels and noise families (skew-normal and GNO, including skewness beyond what skew-normal can express), evaluates against many relevant baselines on 13 established benchmarks, reports AUDRC alongside accuracy, and includes an honest ablation on KDE marginals (Tables 11-16).

Useful multivariate extension with a correct and simple Proposition 5.1 (with proof) that reduces scoring effort to nodes with unoriented edges, and strong multivariate results (Table 2, Table 10) including an oracle-MEC variant that isolates estimation quality from structure-learning quality.
Good reproducibility (public code and experimental runs) and a candid limitations and impact discussion, including identifiability caveats and the Gaussian-marginal assumption of SKEWD-LL.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core estimation machinery is a fairly direct adaptation of the ECM algorithm of Ferreira et al. (2023) to LSNMs with splines; the causal discovery components (RESIT-style independence testing and likelihood scoring) follow standard recipes. The contribution is primarily a new application/model combination rather than a new inference principle.

Concerns about the self-created benchmark: on the novel datasets, SKEWD-LL achieves 100% accuracy everywhere, and notably IGCI-G, which the authors themselves call 'highly misspecified' (it assumes almost deterministic functions), also achieves near-perfect accuracy (Table 5). This suggests the injective sigmoidal data-generating mechanism may contain structural artifacts that favor certain methods, weakening the strength of the 'most reliable under high skewness' claim derived largely from these synthetic datasets.

Model mismatch is handled somewhat asymmetrically: the skew-normal caps skewness at ~0.995, yet one benchmark tier uses skewness 1.750 with heavier tails (GNO), where the model is misspecified; perfect SKEWD-LL performance there is surprising and deserves deeper analysis rather than being framed as robustness. Conversely, on the 13 established benchmarks SKEWD-LL (the headline variant) trails ROCHE and even SKEWD-IT, so 'on par with SOTA' holds mainly for the independence-testing variant.

Heavy and fragile pipeline: parameter estimation requires Bayesian optimization of penalty parameters plus a stochastic CMA-ES heuristic followed by ECM refinement, with many hyperparameters (spline dimensions, iteration caps, bounds, special-casing of Tübingen pair 69). Runtime and sensitivity to this machinery are not systematically quantified, and scalability of SKEWD-MV is admittedly restricted to small/sparse problems.

The Gaussian-marginal assumption underlying likelihood scoring is theoretically awkward (if the noise is skew-normal, the effect's marginal is not normal; standardization does not make a skewed marginal Gaussian), and Proposition A.1 addresses only asymptotic standardization, not the adequacy of the marginal-likelihood comparison; the KDE ablation shows this matters in practice, but the resolution is left to future work.

Minor presentation issues: e.g., Appendix A.2 contains a typo ('the cause given its effects is modeled as Y|X'), and the notation/tables are dense; some claims in Figure 2's caption (IGCI-G bias) are noted but not investigated.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: prior LSNM-based causal discovery methods (LOCI, ROCHE, GRCI, etc.) assume symmetric noise, and the paper convincingly demonstrates (Figure 1, Figure 2/Table 5) that this assumption causes systematic failures as skewness increases.

The estimation methodology is technically careful: the authors adapt the ECM algorithm of Ferreira et al. (2023) to a penalized skew-normal GAM setting, handle known difficulties of skew-normal ML (unbounded likelihood, stationary point at λ=0) via reparameterization, CMA-ES initialization, and penalization, and provide an ablation (Tables 3–4) showing the ECM refinement step is indeed necessary.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: six novel skewed benchmark variants, 13 established benchmarks (including the real-world Tübingen collection), both accuracy and AUDRC, multiple ablations (ECM vs. heuristic, KDE vs. Gaussian marginals), and a multivariate proof-of-concept with additional precision/recall/F1 metrics.

Limitations and failure cases are reported honestly: SKEWD-LL performs poorly on Tübingen (45.97%) and this is visible rather than hidden; the marginal-Gaussian assumption is discussed and ablated; scalability constraints of SKEWD-MV are stated explicitly.

Reproducibility is supported by a public implementation and detailed hyperparameter descriptions (Appendix B.1), and an impact statement that honestly identifies the confounding/assumption risks is included.
weaknesses: The headline claim ('most reliable approach under high skewness') rests substantially on the authors' own novel benchmarks, whose skew-normal noise cases exactly match SKEWD's modeling assumption. While the GNO variants add distributional mismatch, the benchmark design partly favors the proposed method; notably, the fully misspecified IGCI-G also achieves near-perfect accuracy on these datasets, which the paper itself acknowledges as 'biased toward the correct direction,' undermining the significance of SKEWD's perfect scores there.

On established benchmarks, SKEWD is not the best method: ROCHE dominates on mean accuracy/AUDRC (Table 1, Table 9), and SKEWD-LL is clearly weakest among LSNM methods on the real-world Tübingen data (45.97%), consistent with the restrictive Gaussian-marginal assumption of the likelihood variant. The practical advantage is therefore confined to a (self-defined) skewness regime.

No runtime or computational-cost comparison is reported in the main text, despite the pipeline involving Bayesian optimization over penalty parameters, multi-start CMA-ES, and an ECM refinement with up to 5000 iterations. Given that scalability is admitted as a limitation of SKEWD-MV, the absence of timing data makes it hard to judge the cost–benefit trade-off against faster baselines like ROCHE or GRCI.

Originality is moderate: the skew-normal distribution, its latent-variable representation, and the ECM machinery are all imported from the statistics literature (Azzalini; Ferreira & Paula; Ferreira et al.); the contribution is the adaptation to LSNMs and the causal-discovery pipeline. Proposition 5.1 is a straightforward consequence of standard MEC properties and does not add much technical depth.

The multivariate evaluation is only a proof of concept on synthetic data generated under the paper's own skew-normal assumption (λ=0.985), with no comparison to ROCHE/GRCI-style robust alternatives in the multivariate setting, and no real-data validation of SKEWD-MV.

The benchmark construction combines skew-normal and GNO datasets purely by matching marginal skewness (γ1) while the tail/kurtosis behavior differs substantially (as the authors note), which conflates skewness robustness with tail-robustness and makes the interpretation of the three 'skewness levels' less clean than suggested.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a concrete, plausible failure mode (skewed noise violating the symmetry assumption in LSNM-based causal discovery) and illustrates it clearly with Figure 1 / Figure 3, where the misspecified normal model produces cause-dependent residuals and a wrong direction inference.

Technically solid methodology: the skew-normal LSNM formulation is clean, the ECM algorithm is carefully adapted from Ferreira et al. (2023) with explicit E-step and CM-step updates, and the combination of CMA-ES initialization with ECM refinement is justified by an ablation (Tables 3-4) showing the refinement is genuinely necessary, particularly for independence testing (up to 28-34% accuracy gains).

The new skew-noise benchmarks are a useful community contribution: they span multiple skewness levels, include noise families (GNO) that go beyond the skew-normal's bounded skewness (|gamma_1| <= 0.995) and tail behavior, and test robustness to model misspecification rather than only the exact assumed model.

Extensive evaluation: 13 established benchmarks, 6 novel skewed datasets, many SOTA baselines (LOCI, ROCHE, GRCI, QCCD, CAM, RESIT, IGCI, CAREFL in supplementary), both accuracy and AUDRC metrics, and a multivariate proof-of-concept with additional precision/recall/F1 results and an oracle-MEC variant that isolates skeleton-estimation error.

Additional ablations (KDE marginals, ECM vs. heuristic-only) are informative and honestly reported, including cases where the alternative (KDE) does worse or where Gaussian marginals win; Proposition 5.1 with proof is a simple but useful efficiency result.
Reproducibility is well addressed: public code and experimental runs, detailed hyperparameter settings, hardware description, and an honest limitations and impact discussion.
weaknesses: The headline gains are demonstrated primarily on the authors' own synthetic datasets, whose generative process (skew-normal/GNO noise) is closely aligned with SKEWD's assumed model class; it is somewhat expected that methods designed for symmetric noise degrade there. On established benchmarks, SKEWD does not outperform the prior SOTA (ROCHE: 87.69% vs. SKEWD-LL 77.43%, SKEWD-IT 85.02%), so the practical advantage outside the new benchmarks is 'on par' rather than superior.

IGCI-G achieves essentially perfect accuracy on the skewed datasets (Tables 5-6) despite being 'strongly misspecified,' which undercuts the claim that SKEWD-LL is 'the only method to achieve perfect accuracy' and raises questions about how diagnostic the new benchmark is for model-based approaches in general. The authors' explanation (bias toward the correct direction) deserves a more careful analysis.

The justification for neglecting marginal log-likelihoods in SKEWD-LL (Appendix A.3, Proposition A.1) is technically problematic: the sum of squared standardized observations equals n-1 exactly for any data, so the argument does not require nor establish that the marginals are Gaussian; treating standardized data as 'approximately standard normal in large samples' is incorrect for non-Gaussian distributions. The practical consequence (the marginal term cancels in the comparison) is fine, but the stated probabilistic claim is wrong, and the Gaussian-marginal assumption's effect on the joint likelihood comparison is conflated with the fixed plug-in value.

The multivariate evaluation is limited to synthetic data generated with skew-normal noise matching the method's assumption (lambda = 0.985), moderate sizes (d = 6, 10, sparse Erdos-Renyi graphs), and a likelihood-based extension that depends on PC skeleton/MEC quality; scalability is acknowledged to be a serious constraint (exponential in undirected degree, PCCs ~40 at d = 10), and there is no evaluation on real multivariate data.

Computational cost is high (Bayesian optimization with k-fold CV + CMA-ES with large populations + ECM with up to 5000 iterations per conditional), and no systematic runtime comparison against baselines is reported, making the cost-benefit trade-off hard to assess.

No real-world case study exhibiting skewed noise is provided, despite the motivation citing real skewed phenomena (coastal flooding, rainfall); the Tübingen results (45.97% for SKEWD-LL) suggest the Gaussian-marginal likelihood variant struggles on real data, which weakens the transfer of the synthetic conclusions to practice.
